segments.title: French dreadnought design met the limits of its shipyards
segments.body: French designers reached the dreadnought era just as their yards had caught up with the last pre-dreadnought generation. Courbet was a serviceable first-generation dreadnought design delivered after that generation had passed, and Bretagne repeated the problem in the super-dreadnought category. Expectations of short battles kept gun elevation low, leaving some French ships unable to engage much beyond 12,000-13,000 yards. Larger slipways and dry docks were needed before designers could escape the size limits of the existing infrastructure. Normandie and Lyon retained 340 mm guns and added barrels as foreign guns and protection grew heavier. France also had to fund a large modern army facing Germany, so its naval designs reflected limited money as well as limited yards.

evidence.note: French design chronology, low gun elevation, restricted docks, 340 mm batteries, and competing army expenditure.

segments.summary: Courbet and Bretagne arrived behind their design generation, while short-range doctrine, restricted yards, and army commitments constrained their successors.

segments.title: Normandie and Lyon stretched France's investment in 340 mm guns
segments.body: A successor armed with eight 15-inch guns threatened to exceed the dimensions of France's existing yards and docks. Developing another new gun would also be expensive after the 340 mm weapon had equipped only the Bretagne class. Normandie therefore sought comparable firepower through twelve smaller guns in quadruple turrets. The choice has a parallel in the American decision to increase the number of 14-inch guns when a 16-inch weapon was refused. Lyon extended the idea to sixteen 340 mm guns, but its expected contemporaries would be protected against 14-, 15-, or possibly 16-inch fire. Retaining the existing calibre reduced development demands while making penetration of newer protection increasingly doubtful.

evidence.note: Dock dimensions, the limited 340 mm production run, twelve-gun Normandie, and Lyon's sixteen-gun response to stronger foreign protection.

segments.summary: Restricted yards and a short production run encouraged France to retain 340 mm guns, first in twelve-gun Normandie and then in sixteen-gun Lyon.

segments.title: Normandie's mixed engines complicated training and protection
segments.body: Courbet and Bretagne had already adopted turbines, but Normandie combined turbines with vertical triple-expansion engines in pursuit of efficiency. France's main naval opponent was nearby, weakening the case for accepting that complexity to improve long-distance operation. American experiments at least assigned the different propulsion systems to separate ships; the French arrangement required one crew to operate both. Vertical triple-expansion engines also occupied considerable height inside the hull. Their dimensions affected machinery spaces, protection, and turret placement, adding a design cost beyond the proposed fuel saving.

evidence.note: The mixed propulsion decision, nearby French naval threat, crew training, and the height of vertical triple-expansion engines.

segments.summary: Combining turbines and vertical triple-expansion engines required two operating skills and a machinery layout that accommodated the taller engines.

segments.title: More guns help only while their shells can penetrate
segments.body: More barrels give a penetrating weapon more opportunities to hit. The useful calibre therefore depends on the enemy protection and the distance at which battle is expected. Lyon illustrates the limit of multiplying an existing weapon: sixteen 340 mm guns would still face opponents designed to resist heavier shells. Increasing the battery cannot solve inadequate penetration.

evidence.note: The recalled smaller-versus-larger-guns question and the penetration threshold used to answer it.

segments.summary: Gun numbers increase the chances of a hit, but the shell must first be capable of penetrating the intended opponent.
segments.question: Is it better to have more smaller guns or fewer bigger guns?
segments.answerShort: Choose more guns while their shells can penetrate the expected enemy protection at normal battle ranges. Once they cannot, a larger calibre is needed.

segments.title: Why favour a 16.5-inch battleship gun?
segments.body: The preference for 16.5-inch guns rests on keeping a high rate of fire at a large calibre. Beyond that size, the loading cycle is expected to reduce the frequency of salvos sharply. With visual fire control, each salvo helps establish the opponent's position and correct the range, so slower firing also delays adjustment. A super-heavy 16.5-inch shell is suggested as a way to increase hitting power without moving to a larger gun. Armour capable of resisting such a shell is judged to demand an exceptionally heavily protected ship.

evidence.note: The recalled best-calibre question, preference for 16.5 inches, possible super-heavy shells, and the value of salvo frequency for visual ranging.

segments.summary: A personal preference for 16.5-inch guns rests on penetration and the frequent salvos needed to correct visual fire control.
segments.question: What is the best calibre for a battleship gun?
segments.answerShort: The preference offered is 16.5 inches, combining heavy penetration with a useful rate of fire before larger weapons impose a substantial loading penalty.

segments.title: Germany's battleship pause shaped the balance at Jutland
segments.body: Germany's battleship construction pause allowed Britain to establish an eight-to-twelve-ship lead before the Bayern class was laid down. Four Königs faced a British programme of twelve 13.5-inch super-dreadnoughts, followed by the Queen Elizabeth and Revenge classes. The shift of money back to the German army interrupted the naval sequence while British building continued. Bayern and Baden were contemporary with the Revenges, whereas the Queen Elizabeths belonged to the previous year's programme and had a useful speed advantage. Even a favourable assessment of a Bayern in an individual duel could not make two ships answer the ten British 15-inch ships completed, with thirteen originally planned. Britain also retained spare shipyard capacity and private armament development beyond the Royal Navy's own orders.

evidence.note: German construction gaps, competing army budgets, Bayern's contemporaries, British numerical superiority, and spare industrial capacity.

segments.summary: Germany built four Königs and then paused while Britain established a much larger force of 13.5-inch and 15-inch battleships.
segments.question: When did Germany effectively lose Jutland?
segments.answerShort: In this interpretation, Germany's position at Jutland was undermined in 1912, as budget decisions opened a construction gap while Britain continued building super-dreadnoughts.

segments.title: British yards still lacked orders during the dreadnought race
segments.body: British yards built export battleships for South American customers while supplying the Royal Navy's dreadnought programme. Even that combined demand left some firms seeking orders, and Thames Ironworks closed despite having built an Orion-class battleship. The argument is that government purchasing decisions limited output more than physical capacity did. A counterfactual programme with more early British dreadnoughts is proposed as a way to make a German numerical challenge appear futile. Germany could still compete through the quality of individual ships, but Britain's available yard capacity made a contest in total numbers difficult to sustain.

evidence.note: Export orders, unused British yards, Thames Ironworks, and the proposed effect of a larger early Royal Navy building programme.

segments.summary: Export battleships and the Royal Navy's programme still left British construction capacity unused, with Thames Ironworks closing for lack of work.

segments.title: Private gun development outpaced conservative Royal Navy orders
segments.body: The Royal Navy declined some opportunities to adopt triple turrets or move earlier to heavier guns. The St Vincent class is cited as a case where 13.5-inch guns were available as a choice, yet the navy retained 12-inch weapons. While the 15-inch gun was under development, private firms were already marketing a 16-inch gun to Brazil. British companies still built full-size battleship guns on speculation, hoping to sell them either to the navy or to foreign customers. That commercial development gave Britain alternatives beyond the equipment ordered for its current fleet, while German practice centred on Krupp and a more conservative progression from 12-inch to 15-inch guns.

evidence.note: Conservative British gun choices, private 16-inch export marketing, speculative gun manufacture, and comparison with German development.

segments.summary: British armament firms developed heavy guns for possible naval and export sales while the Royal Navy often chose more conservative designs.

segments.title: L20 Alpha belongs beside wartime British design studies
segments.body: L20 and the other late German capital-ship proposals were credible designs for 1916-17. Queen Elizabeth had been designed around 1911-12, so comparing the two gives Germany several years of development without allowing Britain a response. The gap is compared with the interval between St Vincent and Queen Elizabeth, during which British battleship capability changed considerably. Germany had not completed Mackensen or the later Bayern-class ships, making service around 1920-21 an optimistic prospect even if the war and construction continued. British alternatives included revised Queen Elizabeth concepts and heavier derivatives of Hood, using machinery and gun development already under way. These remain proposed responses, while Germany's blockade and major land war made building its own paper designs increasingly difficult.

evidence.note: The 1911-12 versus 1916-17 design gap, unfinished German capital ships, and proposed British replies using existing development work.

segments.summary: L20 and Ersatz Yorck belong beside Britain's wartime design work, several years after Queen Elizabeth's design freeze.

segments.title: Revised Queen Elizabeth designs offered several replies to L20
segments.body: One proposed reply is a repeat Queen Elizabeth with small-tube boilers, estimated at about 28 knots while retaining eight 15-inch guns. The alternative ten-gun design originally considered for Queen Elizabeth offers another starting point. Its original speed is corrected to roughly 20-22 knots, rising to an estimated 25-26 knots with improved boilers before further machinery or hull work. Lengthening that design for ten 16-inch guns is then projected to yield 27-28 knots with substantial belt protection. An eight-gun 16.5-inch variant would remove one turret and release length for more machinery, suggesting a still faster battleship. These are conditional design exercises assembled from existing British development work, and their quoted speeds are estimates for the proposed combinations.

evidence.note: Small-tube-boiler Queen Elizabeth variants, correction of the original ten-gun design's speed, and projected 16- and 16.5-inch alternatives.

segments.summary: Small-tube boilers, heavier guns, and changes in turret count produce several proposed British responses to a German L20 programme.

segments.title: Hood's wartime design could underpin a heavier British response
segments.body: Hood is often thought of as a postwar ship, but her original design was complete and construction had begun before Jutland. Changes after the battle increased protection, continuing revisions that were already under way. Her combination of high speed, eight 15-inch guns, and protection comparable with Queen Elizabeth shows what British designers were pursuing in late 1915 and early 1916. A proposed response to the German paper battleships takes that lineage and adds heavier armour, accepting a fall in speed. Replacing the 15-inch turrets with 16.5-inch weapons is then estimated to leave a ship of about 28 knots with a heavier inclined belt. Stronger internal structure and subdivision would be required to carry the additions, so this remains a proposed derivative rather than a specification for the historical Hood.

evidence.note: Hood's pre-Jutland design and construction, subsequent protection changes, and the proposed structural and armament changes for a heavier derivative.

segments.summary: Hood's pre-Jutland origins provide a second starting point for a proposed battleship with heavier armour and 16.5-inch guns.

segments.title: British industry could answer credible German designs
segments.body: The German studies of 1916 and 1917 were credible designs near the contemporary technical frontier. Germany nevertheless had to fund naval construction while under blockade and fighting a major land war against several armies. Britain's broader network of shipbuilders and armament firms gave it more opportunities to adopt an improvement and develop a stronger response. The earlier ironclad race offers a comparison: France could produce capable ships, while British industrial capacity supported larger numbers and continued development. Technical competence alone did not give Germany the resources to sustain another round of construction.

evidence.note: Credible German designs, wartime resource constraints, and Britain's ability to answer foreign improvements through multiple shipbuilding and armament firms.

segments.summary: Germany's advanced designs faced wartime production constraints, while Britain's larger network of yards and armament firms could support further development.

segments.title: G3 and N3 as a warning against another naval race
segments.body: One interpretation of G3 and N3 centres on making rival governments reluctant to challenge British naval strength. The comparison is with the late Victorian Admiral-class ironclads, whose appearance could discourage an opponent from testing its fleet in battle. Earlier studies with heavier armament and higher performance gave the Royal Navy options beyond the reduced G3 and N3 designs. The financial argument distinguishes Britain's postwar debt from an inability to build: declining debt and existing industrial capacity are offered as reasons that government spending choices mattered. In this reading, the warning was that Britain could still build several formidable ships and respond to further competition with stronger designs.

evidence.note: The Admiral-class deterrence analogy, stronger predecessors to G3 and N3, and the argument that postwar British construction depended on government spending choices.

segments.summary: One interpretation connects the proposed ships with the deterrent reputation of the Admiral-class ironclads and Britain's ability to develop still stronger designs.

segments.title: Lexington prompted new docks while British designs had to fit existing bases
segments.body: The American Lexington programme included investment in docks large enough to support its exceptionally long battlecruisers. The Philadelphia dry dock later used by New Jersey is cited as a surviving result of that decision. Britain could build and maintain its larger capital-ship studies at some facilities, but only a limited number of docks could accommodate them. Supporting those ships across the empire would have required further spending on overseas infrastructure. British designers consequently reduced their proposals to fit a wider existing network, including abandoning efforts to carry nine 18-inch guns in a battlecruiser of acceptable dimensions. A six-gun alternative could fit, but its main battery was judged too small.

evidence.note: Lexington-related dock investment, the Philadelphia example, Britain's limited number of suitable docks, and reductions needed to fit capital ships into the existing global network.

segments.summary: The contrast explains why infrastructure spending allowed American designs to grow while Britain's worldwide basing requirements pushed G3 and N3 towards smaller forms.

segments.title: K3 and L3 combined nine 18-inch guns with different speed priorities
segments.body: The K3 and L3 studies show the scale of British ambitions before the final G3 and N3 proposals. Both are described with nine 18-inch guns and normal displacement around 50,000 tons. K3's battlecruiser requirement called for 30 knots, while the smaller L3 battleship was intended for 25 knots. The quoted L3 protection includes a 15-inch main belt inclined at 25 degrees, a nine-inch upper belt and eight-inch deck armour. Both designs are given 18-inch turret faces, supported by British presses and earlier Vickers experiments with plates of that thickness. If construction had proceeded before a later treaty, these ships or their smaller descendants would have left Britain with a substantially different fleet entering the 1930s.

evidence.note: The K3 and L3 displacement, armament, speed and armour figures, British thick-plate manufacturing capability, and the counterfactual effect of completing such ships before a later treaty.

segments.summary: The larger British studies paired heavy armament with either battlecruiser speed or stronger battleship protection, backed by existing armour-manufacturing capacity.

segments.title: Interwar closures reduced Britain's wartime shipbuilding workforce
segments.body: Clarke and Drachinifel blame Treasury-backed shipyard closures for weakening Britain's ability to rearm. Their examples include Palmers at Jarrow, the dispersal of heavy equipment, and covenants said to prohibit renewed naval construction for decades. They connect the loss of work at Jarrow with the Jarrow March and argue that closures continued even after the ten-year rule ended and rearmament funding resumed. The damage extended beyond empty slipways because trained workers also left the industry. Vanguard and Implacable illustrate the later consequence: berths existed for both, but the available skilled workforce could not complete both at once, so the carrier received priority. Retaining yards and supporting workers through the downturn is proposed as an alternative that could have preserved capacity for wartime expansion.

evidence.note: The criticism of Treasury-backed closures, Palmers and Jarrow, restrictive covenants, continued losses during rearmament, and the workforce choice between Vanguard and Implacable.

segments.summary: Yard closures, equipment sales and restrictions on rebuilding are blamed for the shortage of skilled labour that later forced choices between major warships.

segments.title: Should Britain have chosen F3 instead of Nelson and Rodney?
segments.body: Nelson and Rodney are admired for their service, but their 16-inch armament is questioned as a prestige response to the Nagato and Colorado classes. F3 would have provided a fully armoured battlecruiser with a new 15-inch gun. That weapon also offered a possible improvement for older British ships already armed with guns of the same calibre. The treaty argument distinguishes increasing calibre from installing an improved gun of the existing calibre. American improvements to the 14-inch guns of the standard battleships supply the comparison, while a British 15-inch/45 or possible 15-inch/50 remains a proposed development rather than an upgrade that actually occurred.

evidence.note: The explicit F3-versus-Nelson question, preference for the faster design, and the proposed use of improved same-calibre guns under treaty restrictions.

segments.summary: The F3 alternative offered a fast, well-protected ship and a possible route to improving the guns of older British capital ships without increasing their calibre.
segments.question: Should the Royal Navy have built F3 rather than Nelson and Rodney?
segments.answerShort: Both historians favour F3 for its combination of speed, protection and improved 15-inch guns, while questioning how much the Nelsons owed to the wish to match foreign 16-inch ships.

segments.title: An early replacement bargain could have produced four F3s
segments.body: The proposed treaty bargain would exchange Britain's claim to new 16-inch ships for permission to replace Renown and Repulse early. Their speed and armament remained useful, but their protection was weaker than that of the Queen Elizabeths, R-class and Hood even after the addition of nine-inch armour. Early-replacement provisions granted to France and Italy supply the suggested precedent. Two F3s in place of Nelson and Rodney, followed by two more to replace the Renowns, would leave four F3s alongside Hood. Five fast capital ships could ordinarily support a four-ship operational division while one was unavailable. The scenario would also give Britain a fleet with more consistent protection and 15-inch armament, but depends on a negotiated concession that was never obtained.

evidence.note: The proposed exchange of 16-inch parity for early Renown and Repulse replacements, the French and Italian precedent, and the resulting force of four F3s with Hood.

segments.summary: Replacing Renown and Repulse after building two initial F3s could have supplied a five-ship fast force with more consistent protection.

segments.title: Vanguard and F3 expose competing definitions of fast battleship
segments.body: One historian calls Vanguard a fully armoured battlecruiser, distinguishing it from the King George V and Lion designs described as British fast battleships. The other uses fast battleship more broadly for a ship capable of fighting in the line while maintaining high speed. They also dispute whether that broad threshold should be about 25 or 28 knots. Scharnhorst, Dunkerque and the rebuilt Cavour and Duilio classes enter the comparison because their capabilities fit the wider category. Hood and the proposed F3s are judged capable opponents for those ships, especially if the hypothetical F3 armament included improved 15-inch guns. The disagreement concerns the meaning assigned to the category as well as the ships' physical capabilities.

evidence.note: Competing definitions of Vanguard and F3, the disputed speed threshold, and comparisons with German, French and rebuilt Italian capital ships.

segments.summary: The historians disagree over whether British design categories or a broader combination of battle-line capability and speed should determine the label.

segments.title: F3's forward battery and speed change two German encounters
segments.body: Replacing Renown with an F3 in its encounter with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau would bring nine guns to bear forward in place of four. Better seakeeping is also credited with making the proposed ship a stronger opponent. The comparison then moves to Operation Berlin, when Rodney nearly caught Gneisenau. An F3's stated 28-knot speed is judged sufficient to make escape much harder in that encounter. These are specific counterfactual uses of the design's forward armament and speed, with the outcome depending on substituting an unbuilt ship for the historical British opponent.

evidence.note: The proposed nine-gun forward engagement in place of Renown, F3 seakeeping, and the judgement that a 28-knot F3 could catch Gneisenau during Operation Berlin.

segments.summary: Two encounters with Scharnhorst and Gneisenau test how F3's nine forward-firing guns and higher speed could affect pursuit and combat.

segments.title: Emergency speed consumes machinery life
segments.body: A steam plant's design speed assumes that its machinery will survive years of service with regular maintenance. Higher output first shortens the distance between maintenance periods, then consumes machinery life, and can eventually make a major refit or sudden failure an accepted risk. The practical limit also depends on turbine strength, shafts, propellers, cavitation and the resistance of the hull. Samuel B. Roberts at Samar and Rodney during the Bismarck chase illustrate why crews might accept those costs when survival or interception depends on speed. An experienced engineering team has to judge how much more its particular plant can deliver. Fuel exhaustion, boiler failure and damage to the turbines or propellers impose different limits on how long that effort can continue.

evidence.note: Successive maintenance and failure margins, structural limits on transmitting extra power, and emergency-speed examples involving Samuel B. Roberts and Rodney.

segments.summary: An engineering crew can extract additional speed by accepting shorter maintenance intervals, permanent wear and an increasing risk of machinery failure.

segments.title: Samuel B. Roberts combined a lighter displacement with a capable hull
segments.body: Samuel B. Roberts provides a specific example of why hull form and displacement matter when a ship exceeds its rated speed. Its John C. Butler-class hull is compared with the heavier destroyer-escort designs developed for turbo-electric machinery. The explanation gives roughly the same length-to-beam ratio and nominal power, but around 1,350 tons rather than approximately 1,750 tons. Removing about 400 tons from a hull intended to reach 24 knots at the greater displacement left more room for performance. Driving the machinery harder could then exploit that lighter load, provided the hull and propulsion system could accept the additional power. The figures are the explanation offered for Roberts' emergency-speed margin, rather than a new trial measurement.

evidence.note: The comparison of John C. Butler-class hull proportions, approximately 400 tons less displacement, similar nominal power, and the resulting capacity for emergency speed.

segments.summary: The proposed explanation for Roberts' extra speed combines a hull designed for a heavier ship with reduced displacement and heavily driven machinery.

segments.title: How much does cruising speed change a fleet's transit time?
segments.body: The New York-to-San Diego comparison gives nearly 21 days at 10 knots, 16.9 days at 12 knots, and a little over 14 days at 14 knots. A modest improvement in cruising speed therefore removes several days from a long deployment. At the higher example speeds, the estimates are 9.6 days at 21 knots and 8.4 days at 24 knots. Maximum speed remains useful for manoeuvring in battle, while strategic movement depends on the speed a force can sustain over the voyage. Nuclear-powered American carriers provide a later example of sustained high cruising speed. Their escorts also needed sufficient endurance and power to maintain that pace, which supplies the connection to nuclear cruisers.

evidence.note: The explicit transit-time question, estimates for 10, 12, 14, 21 and 24 knots, and the connection between sustained speed and nuclear-powered carrier escorts.

segments.summary: Transit estimates show why sustained cruising speed can determine when a fleet reaches its theatre of operations.
segments.question: What difference does cruising at 10 rather than 12 knots make on a voyage from New York to San Diego through the Panama Canal?
segments.answerShort: The estimates are nearly 21 days at 10 knots and 16.9 days at 12 knots, so two additional cruising knots save several days.

segments.title: Daring's 30-knot rating included war loads and months out of dock
segments.body: The postwar British design documents described here rate speed under demanding service conditions: full wartime loading, six months out of dry dock and tropical temperatures. A battleship expected to maintain 30 knots in those circumstances could need the power to reach roughly 35 knots when new and more lightly loaded. The Daring-class destroyers supply a practical comparison because their stated 30 knots was presented as a speed they could guarantee under those adverse conditions. Better conditions allowed higher speeds without making the service rating misleading. An anecdote claims that a freshly prepared Daring reached 43 knots when its captain wanted to demonstrate the ship to his father. That figure came from a diary entry which the historian explicitly says he could not verify, so it remains an unconfirmed example.

evidence.note: Service-condition speed ratings, the Daring guarantee at full war load in tropical conditions, and a 43-knot diary anecdote explicitly described as unverified.

segments.summary: Conservative service guarantees explain why a Royal Navy speed rating could sit well below performance in favourable conditions.

segments.title: Froude's hull research helped ships exceed their rated speed
segments.body: Froude's experimental tanks and hull-form research are credited with giving British designers an early advantage. A hull designed to work efficiently above the ship's published speed leaves room to benefit from additional power. That capability can remain unused until circumstances demand more than normal service performance. Reports of such occasions may remain classified or meet disbelief because they exceed the familiar specification. The underwater shape therefore matters when assessing claims that a ship performed beyond its nominal rating.

evidence.note: Froude's experimental work, hull forms capable of higher speeds, and the limited visibility or disputed reception of exceptional performance.

segments.summary: Experimental tanks and efficient underwater forms could give a ship useful performance beyond the speed listed in its specifications.

segments.title: Rodney's trials and hull lineage challenge a fixed speed ceiling
segments.body: Rodney's disputed 25-knot speed during the Bismarck chase is compared with her trial performance, which came within 0.8 knots of that figure. Iowa's ability to exceed a nominal 33 knots is generally accepted, although Nelson and Rodney exceeded their own design speeds by a greater margin on trials. F3 and the Nelson design shared closely related hull forms developed from Britain's larger, faster capital-ship studies. Those earlier studies had addressed ships displacing roughly half as much again and travelling at 32-33 knots. Applying that research to a smaller, slower requirement could leave speed available beyond the guaranteed figure. In an emergency, the remaining constraint could be the machinery life the navy was willing to sacrifice.

evidence.note: Rodney's trial speed, comparison with Iowa, and the F3/Nelson hull lineage support the argument for speed beyond the published rating.

segments.summary: Rodney's trial performance and the hull research behind F3 support the argument that published speed left an emergency reserve.

segments.title: Sloop movements and aerial identification suggest unused speed
segments.body: In the June 1939 example, a sloop rated at 20 knots reportedly left with a Town-class cruiser, remained in station and arrived at the same time. The argument for greater speed rests on that shared timetable and the absence of any reported separation. A second example concerns Johnnie Walker's sloops in the Bay of Biscay, where German reconnaissance identified the formation as a British cruiser squadron. Turning towards the aircraft in a battle line presented a profile with three twin mountings, comparable to an Arethusa-class cruiser. Apparent speed is treated as another reason the pilots accepted that identification. The resulting report discouraged a German destroyer attack against the much smaller force. Neither example supplies a measured maximum speed, but both challenge treating a published rating as an absolute limit.

evidence.note: A June 1939 sloop-and-cruiser timetable and Walker's reported misidentification as a cruiser squadron support an inference of speed beyond published ratings.

segments.summary: A sloop keeping station with a cruiser and Johnnie Walker's formation being mistaken for cruisers provide two arguments for looking beyond rated speed.

segments.title: Treaty compliance could leave room for later armour and emergency power
segments.body: A navy could comply with declared limits while benefiting from the way those limits were defined. Standard displacement is one example of a rule whose wording could favour particular requirements. A ship could also meet its published specification while carrying machinery limitations or provision for equipment to be fitted later. Drachinifel suspects that the County-class hulls were deliberately designed to accept a subsequent belt of about 4.5 inches. The completed cruisers could still meet their original 10,000-ton declaration with box protection and eight 8-inch guns. Emergency bypass valves and additional boiler fuel feeds provide a separate example of reserve power concealed within otherwise defensible machinery arrangements.

evidence.note: Treaty definitions, the suspected County-class allowance for later belt armour, and emergency boiler arrangements illustrate different ways to retain capability beyond the declared specification.

segments.summary: Loading definitions, provision for later armour and emergency machinery arrangements could preserve capability beyond what a navy demonstrated publicly.

segments.title: Mackensen intelligence helped shape the Admiral-class response
segments.body: Mackensen's 350 mm guns and 28-knot design made it a credible fast capital ship. Its threat to Britain depended partly on the absence of a 15-inch successor to Tiger. Tiger's denser subdivision and greater armour coverage suggest a different route to an Admiral-class design than following Renown's principles. In that counterfactual, building 15-inch ships on Tiger's principles might have reduced redesign work enough to complete all four Admirals during the war. The historical Admirals emerged from a shallow-draught Queen Elizabeth requirement and British intelligence that incorrectly credited Mackensen with 15-inch guns. Hood consequently offered heavier firepower, somewhat greater speed and strong protection against the actual Mackensen design. The reported German specification more closely resembled Ersatz Yorck.

evidence.note: Mackensen's armament and speed, the proposed Tiger-derived alternative, and the mistaken 15-inch intelligence report explain the Admiral-class comparison.

segments.summary: Overstated reports of Mackensen's armament helped produce a British response with more firepower and speed than the German ship actually required.

segments.title: Intelligence can reveal a successor while its predecessor is being built
segments.body: A warship's design had to be frozen early enough to order items with long manufacturing lead times. By the time its keel was laid, work on the next year's successor should already be well advanced. An intelligence request for the latest German battlecruiser concept could therefore uncover plans newer than the Mackensen design entering construction. This offers a possible explanation for British reports that looked more like Ersatz Yorck than Mackensen. It remains an interpretation of the mismatch, rather than proof that a particular design study was obtained. Ersatz Yorck's heavier armament also came with a lower official speed of 27 knots and little additional protection, leaving it disadvantaged against the Admirals.

evidence.note: Design freezes, advance ordering and annual successor work provide a possible explanation for the Mackensen intelligence mismatch; Ersatz Yorck's 27-knot speed limits the comparison.

segments.summary: Annual construction schedules meant the latest German battlecruiser concept could differ substantially from the design already on the slipway.

segments.title: Ersatz Yorck was a wartime adaptation of Mackensen
segments.body: Ersatz Yorck retained Mackensen's beam, machinery and much of its protection while lengthening the hull by less than 20 feet for 15-inch guns. Its greater weight and largely unchanged power plant explain why this was an adaptation of an existing design. Germany needed a prompt response to newer British ships while its army absorbed much of the wartime budget. Naval designers also had fewer industrial and infrastructure options available. British service priorities generally favoured the navy, whereas the German navy faced pressure from the army if its costs rose too far. The comparison extends to Austria-Hungary, whose fewer ships could still embody substantial qualitative advances. Under these constraints, a limited Mackensen revision was a design the navy could justify in both time and money.

evidence.note: Ersatz Yorck's retained dimensions, machinery and protection reflect wartime resource limits; the comparison contrasts German army priority with British naval priority and Austro-Hungarian qualitative development.

segments.summary: The 15-inch Ersatz Yorck was a rapid enlargement of Mackensen under wartime time, budget, and industrial constraints.

segments.title: Iowa reused South Dakota's design to gain speed quickly
segments.body: Iowa is characterised as a South Dakota design stretched enough to provide substantially greater speed. Its armament changed from 16-inch/45 guns to 16-inch/50 guns. The ships were designed before the United States entered the war, but the prospect of conflict imposed pressure on the programme. Reusing an established design could save time and money compared with starting afresh. More radical Iowa alternatives existed, but the adopted approach illustrates how urgency can favour a practical enlargement over a new design.

evidence.note: The Iowa/South Dakota comparison identifies a lengthened hull, longer 16-inch guns and pressure from approaching war as reasons to adapt an existing design.

segments.summary: The Iowa comparison treats lengthening an existing battleship and fitting longer guns as a response to the pressure of approaching war.

segments.title: A 15-inch Scharnhorst could have accelerated Vanguard
segments.body: Scharnhorst's 11-inch armament reflected both immediate industrial capacity and Hitler's wish to avoid provoking Britain too strongly. Krupp could develop a 15-inch gun, but that required time for an item normally ordered before the ship itself. Arming Scharnhorst with 15-inch guns from the outset would have made the threat harder for Britain to answer: Renown and Repulse had much less armour, Hood was only one ship, and the King George V class could not compel a faster opponent to fight. One proposed response brings Vanguard-type ships into construction alongside the King George V class after earlier investment in armour production. The illustrative ordering sequence pairs a Vanguard with Duke of York, another with Anson and Howe, and a possible third with Lion and Temeraire. Spare 15-inch guns would avoid the new-gun delays expected for the Lions and could let those additional ships finish sooner. These dates form a counterfactual programme whose feasibility depends on earlier infrastructure spending.

evidence.note: Industrial readiness and political caution explain the 11-inch choice; a 15-inch alternative leads to the proposed British armour investment and earlier Vanguard ordering sequence.

segments.summary: Arming Scharnhorst with 15-inch guns from the outset might have pushed Britain toward earlier Vanguard-type ships and expanded armor production.

segments.title: An early Vanguard reshapes the Bismarck chase and Force Z
segments.body: A Vanguard laid down with Duke of York might have finished around the same time as Prince of Wales because its established 15-inch guns required fewer trials. It could then have been available at Scapa Flow when Bismarck sailed, giving the Home Fleet another fast battleship while Hood's machinery was worn. Its effect on Force Z depends on which historical ship it replaces. Replacing Prince of Wales with Vanguard would let the formation use more of Repulse's speed; in the proposed scenario, the Japanese scout would reach their historical position after the ships had moved farther towards Singapore. Replacing Repulse instead would leave the formation limited by Prince of Wales's speed. Vanguard's stronger anti-aircraft armament and torpedo protection would then give it a better chance of surviving the attack, especially with only a finite number of Japanese torpedoes available. That second scenario does not automatically save Prince of Wales, whose stern hit remains potentially fatal unless Vanguard's fire disrupts the attack.

evidence.note: An earlier Vanguard is placed in the Bismarck operation, then tested in two Force Z alternatives: replacing Prince of Wales for speed or replacing Repulse for protection.

segments.summary: The counterfactual tests Vanguard's speed, torpedo defense, and anti-aircraft suite in the Denmark Strait and Malayan campaigns.

segments.title: A faster battle line would pull carrier construction forward
segments.body: Earlier Vanguard construction could create a requirement for another carrier able to accompany the faster surface forces. British carrier roles included scouting and reconnaissance, accompanying moving fleet formations, and strike operations. Older carriers would struggle to keep pace with the additional fast ships. One possible response is another Illustrious-class carrier on Formidable's pattern; another is an earlier Implacable. Under that counterfactual, Force Z might arrive in the Far East with a carrier as well as its capital ships, changing its ability to find an opponent and defend itself from aircraft.

evidence.note: British carrier roles and the need to accompany faster surface groups support the proposed earlier Illustrious or Implacable and a carrier-equipped Force Z.

segments.summary: Early Vanguards would create demand for carriers able to scout for, protect, and keep pace with faster surface formations.

segments.title: A renewed battleship race would expose national bottlenecks
segments.body: A British response to heavier German capital ships would also affect France's programme. French changes could prompt Italy to respond, giving Britain another reason to increase construction. Japan would then reassess the British programme, with consequences for American planning. A counterfactual change can therefore require further reactions rather than leaving every other fleet fixed at its historical strength. The next constraint is what each navy's money and shipbuilding capacity would actually let it do.

evidence.note: The proposed reaction runs through Britain, France, Italy, Japan and the United States before turning to each country's practical building limits.

segments.summary: Changing one German or British program would trigger reactions across several navies rather than leaving the rest of the historical fleet balance fixed.

segments.title: German slipways forced a carrier-versus-battleship tradeoff
segments.body: Germany's reduced naval infrastructure left few slipways suitable for capital ships in the 1930s. Construction of Bismarck and Graf Zeppelin had to fit around the berths released by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. Hurrying ships off those slipways could create additional technical problems without providing more building capacity. Cancelling Graf Zeppelin and carrier B is proposed as one way to release space for another battleship. Those spaces would become available sequentially, so abandoning the carriers would still leave a constrained construction schedule.

evidence.note: Limited large slipways, premature launches and the possible cancellation of the two carriers explain Germany's restricted ability to add capital ships.

segments.summary: Germany could not answer a renewed capital-ship race quickly without giving another major program access to its few large building berths.

segments.title: Italy could enlarge Littorio more easily than fund more hulls
segments.body: Italy had suitable shipbuilding infrastructure but lacked the money for a large expansion of its fleet. In the proposed arms race, a more powerful second Littorio pair offered one way to increase capability without ordering many additional hulls. The second pair's 1938 construction date leaves room in this scenario to reconsider the design. A twelve-gun development could build on existing Italian work and give the ships greater firepower and prestige. It would still require extra money from a government already struggling to finance its naval ambitions.

evidence.note: Italian financial limits, available shipyard infrastructure and a proposed twelve-gun development for the second Littorio pair.

segments.summary: A twelve-gun version of the second Littorio pair offered a possible Italian response to renewed construction abroad, although financing remained difficult.

segments.title: Could Japan answer a renewed arms race with supercruisers?
segments.body: Japan could not simply order more full-size Yamatos because building the historical ships already required extensive yard upgrades. One suggested way to free capacity was to use two yards restricted to commercial work for political reasons. A smaller Yamato study offered another possibility: nine 16-inch guns, roughly 50,000 to 55,000 tons and 28 knots on a hull that could use a smaller slipway. Its protection was expected to substantially exceed that of the contemporary North Carolina and South Dakota designs. More Shokaku-type carriers were another possible response if Japan chose to expand naval aviation instead of its gun battle line. Each option still depended on the facilities Japan could make available.

evidence.note: Japanese yard restrictions, the question about supercruisers, a smaller 16-inch Yamato study and the alternative of additional carriers.

segments.summary: Smaller Yamato studies and additional carriers offered alternatives to building more full-size Yamatos in yards already stretched by the existing programme.
segments.question: Might Japan bring out its supercruiser designs in response to the renewed arms race?
segments.answerShort: Possibly. A smaller Yamato study with nine 16-inch guns or additional Shokaku-type carriers also offered ways to add capital ships within Japan's restricted shipyard capacity.

segments.title: South Dakota's compact layout left narrow deck passages
segments.body: Drachinifel recalls a visible difference between the preserved American battleship classes. North Carolina and the Iowas have space to walk along the side passages despite their numerous twin 5-inch/38 mounts. Massachusetts and Alabama leave much narrower passages beside their secondary batteries. He describes those routes as effectively one-way, making the South Dakota class's compact arrangement apparent to a visitor walking the deck.

evidence.note: Drachinifel's recollection of wider side passages aboard North Carolina and the Iowas and narrow passages aboard Massachusetts and Alabama.

segments.summary: A comparison of preserved battleships shows how the South Dakota class's compact layout restricted movement beside its secondary gun mounts.

segments.title: More North Carolinas offered a quick American response
segments.body: The United States had shipyard capacity for additional capital ships, making repeat construction a practical option in this scenario. North Carolina had already undergone a late change from quadruple 14-inch turrets to triple 16-inch turrets. Another immediate redesign would add work when two more examples of the existing design could be ordered. Their armament would repeat the 16-inch/45 guns and twin 5-inch/38 mounts already being produced. The earlier all-forward North Carolina studies also resemble Britain's F3, with the main turrets concentrated ahead of the superstructure. Those studies show how an established programme could contain several quite different arrangements before reaching its final form.

evidence.note: A proposed four-ship North Carolina programme, existing armament production and the resemblance between its all-forward studies and F3.

segments.summary: Two additional North Carolinas could expand American construction without another immediate redesign.
segments.question: What would the Americans do if the other navies accelerated their capital-ship programmes?
segments.answerShort: A four-ship North Carolina programme was proposed as a quick response, using an existing design and available shipyard capacity.

segments.title: Salamis combined a German hull with foreign naval technology
segments.body: Salamis combined a German-built hull with American 14-inch guns because the German industry did not yet offer the required weapon. Yarrow boilers were selected, with AEG turbines chosen after a planned deal for Parsons turbines could not be arranged. The proposed secondary weapons include 6-inch and 3-inch guns, but their suppliers are identified only tentatively. Drachinifel recommends paying a premium for one exceptionally capable ship when a small navy cannot compete in numbers, forcing a larger opponent to commit several ships against it. Georgios Averof provides the practical comparison: modern equipment and good maintenance helped an armoured cruiser defeat an Ottoman force with heavier ships. Salamis's 14-inch guns promised a range and penetration advantage over the Ottoman ship that became Agincourt. Its belt also offered a plausible defence against Agincourt's 12-inch fire at suitable ranges.

evidence.note: The American main battery, Yarrow boilers, AEG turbines after the failed Parsons arrangement, and uncertain secondary-weapon suppliers, followed by Drachinifel's premium-ship argument and comparisons with Averof and Agincourt.

segments.summary: The Greek dreadnought combined a German hull, American 14-inch guns and Yarrow boilers, while the choice of turbines depended on the suppliers the yard could secure.

segments.title: Greece used a British mission to compare global suppliers
segments.body: Rear Admiral Lionel Grant Tufnell, head of the British naval mission to Greece, supervised the selection process for Salamis. He reviewed ten British, four French, three German, three American, one Austrian and two Italian submissions against the same requirement. After British armour could not be sent to the German yard, he reportedly preferred Bethlehem Steel's product to the German and Italian alternatives. This common evaluation makes the Greek programme a useful comparison of what different suppliers could offer around 1912. Against the Ottoman ship that became Erin, Salamis chiefly offered greater speed: Erin carried two additional main guns, although their calibre was slightly smaller. Maintenance could alter that paper comparison, as Averof's success against the Ottoman Brandenburgs had already shown.

evidence.note: Tufnell's multinational design review and reported armour preferences, followed by Salamis's speed advantage over Erin and the importance of Ottoman maintenance.

segments.summary: Rear Admiral Lionel Grant Tufnell assessed competing designs and armour supplies for Salamis, while the comparison with Erin shows why procurement quality alone could not decide a battle.

segments.title: Export dreadnoughts traded protection for deterrent firepower
segments.body: Many export dreadnoughts sacrificed two or three inches of armour to obtain more firepower, greater speed or a smaller hull. At longer ranges, roughly nine inches of belt armour could still provide useful protection against 12-inch fire and dominate most of a smaller opponent's older fleet. That protection would not keep out contemporary 14- or 15-inch shells. One explanation is that buyers accepted this vulnerability to threaten disproportionate damage with their own heavy guns. Each side might hope to destroy the opposing navy's weaker ships first and then concentrate its surviving fleet against the remaining dreadnoughts. If both sides followed that plan, training, skill and maintenance would help decide which could carry it through.

evidence.note: Reduced protection in export designs, the limits of nine-inch belts and competing plans to destroy an opponent's weaker ships before concentrating against its dreadnoughts.

segments.summary: A roughly nine-inch belt could protect an export dreadnought against much of a regional fleet while leaving it vulnerable to the rival navy's newest heavy guns.

segments.title: Ersatz Monarch was tailored to control the Adriatic
segments.body: Ersatz Monarch resembled Nevada in its ten-gun main battery, with a twin turret superfiring over a triple at each end, and in its 21-knot speed. Its protection and 14-inch guns were well suited to fighting the Italian Cavour and Duilio classes. Four Monarchs operating with the four Tegetthoffs could form a battle line that threatened Italian coastal targets and returned to base without needing to pursue the enemy across the Mediterranean. Faster Italian ships could attempt attacks against part of that line, but the Adriatic offered less room to exploit their speed than the wider Mediterranean basins. A short Austro-Hungarian bombardment sortie might also end before repeated attacks produced results. One damaging salvo could disable an Italian attacker and force other ships to protect it, weakening the opposition to the next sortie. Austro-Hungarian fire control receives credit, while the earlier fleet's turret-ventilation problems are described as having been corrected after the Ancona bombardment.

evidence.note: Ersatz Monarch's layout and intended opponents, the limits of Italian hit-and-run tactics in the Adriatic, and the effect of damaging ships during a short bombardment sortie.

segments.summary: Ten 14-inch guns, credible protection and 21-knot speed made Ersatz Monarch a plausible answer to Italy's existing dreadnoughts in the confined Adriatic.

segments.title: Limited building could have kept battleship design evolving
segments.body: The building holiday restricted the opportunities to develop battleship designs through continued construction. An alternative sketched here would allow Britain and the United States five ships in each five-year period. Smaller allowances for Japan, France and Italy remain tentative, with several possible numbers and intervals mentioned. Continued construction under such limits could have produced a different sequence of designs before the Second World War. The suggestion concerns how regular building changes design development, rather than a settled replacement treaty.

evidence.note: A limited-building counterfactual with five ships per five years for Britain and the United States and tentative smaller allowances for the other powers.

segments.summary: A treaty permitting regular construction could have produced different Second World War battleships by allowing designs to develop through successive programmes.
